newsitem.title: MEXICO: Alfa overcame obstacles in 1996 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Alfa overcame obstacles in 1996 - analysts.

text.p: Mexico's Alfa SA last year was faced with a double whammy -- falling prices for its main products and a strong peso, which held back exports and made dollar revenues less impressive in peso terms.

Despite the obstacles, financial analysts said the industrial company managed to lift operating profits by shifting its focus to the domestic market and increasing output -- a move that some said worked well in 1996 but may be hard to duplicate this year.
"The results were good....These guys were able to have revenue growth in the face of tough conditions," said Terry Sigler, an analyst at Robert Flemings Research in New York.
On Thursday, the Monterrey-based conglomerate said its 1996 net income rose to 3.928 billion pesos from 2.218 billion pesos in 1995.

Earnings per share were 6.55 pesos, slightly less than the average forecast of 6.86 pesos by five industry analysts surveyed by Reuters. Part of the shortfall reflected a fourth-quarter write-off of 216 million pesos related to outdated plants at its Alpek subsidiary.
Much of the increase in profits year-on-year only appeared on the company's books. It reflected non-cash items such as lower foreign exchange losses and monetary gains from inflation.
On an operating basis, profits rose by a more slender 2.7 percent to 4.634 billion pesos for the year. The company said higher sales and a better cost structure were the main reasons.
Alfa, one of Mexico's biggest companies, has five divisions made up of steel (Hylsamex), petrochemicals (Alpek), food (Sigma), telecommunications (Onexa) and retail and auto parts (Versax).

"Increases in the operating income of Hylsamex and Versax, due to higher sales from additional production capacity, more than compensated for a decline in operating income from both Alpek and Sigma, due to less favorable prices in petrochemicals and higher costs of raw materials, respectively," Alfa said in a statement late on Thursday.
The company said all of its units increased volume sales and Hylsamex focused more on the domestic market, which normally has higher margins than exports.

Alfa was hurt by a strong peso, which weakened many of its dollar-linked revenues. In dollar terms, the company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) rose 18.5 percent to $617 million in 1996. In peso terms, the rise was only 5.3 percent to 6.166 billion pesos.

The company's fourth-quarter was less impressive than its performance in the rest of the year. Operating profits slipped during the final three months compared with the third quarter, mostly because of Alpek's weak contribution.
Analysts said the question going forward was whether Alfa would continue to be held back by low steel and petrochemical prices. Hylsamex and Alpek account some 80 percent of revenues.
"They did well, but if (prices) do not recover, then these guys might have a hard time generating enough volume growth to offset that," said one Mexico City analyst.
To be sure, the company has ambitious expansion plans. Alfa is expected to boost capacity at Hylsamex by more than 30 percent in 1998 and inaugurate a new petrochemical plant the same year.
"I view (1997) as more of a year of consolidation, with pretty minor growth in EBITDA. But 1998 and 1999 should be interesting," said Kerry McHugh, an analyst at Goldman Sachs.
